terms.definition: The ceiling- or wall-mounted radio that connects wireless devices to the hospital's wired network.
The family of IEEE standards that defines Wi-Fi. Each generation is an amendment with a letter suffix, such as 802.11ax (Wi-Fi 6) or 802.11be (Wi-Fi 7).
Small battery-powered tags on staff or equipment that report their location so teams can find pumps, wheelchairs or colleagues quickly.
Continuous wireless monitoring of a patient's vital signs, sent from a bedside or wearable monitor to a central station.
A small wearable communicator that lets clinicians call and message each other hands-free over Wi-Fi.
A Wi-Fi 7 feature that lets one connection use links in more than one band at the same time, or switch between them without reconnecting.
A device, client or access point, that can operate several Wi-Fi links as one connection.
A multi-link mode where a device can send on one link while receiving on another, using separate radios.
A multi-link mode where a device cannot send on one link while receiving on another, so link timing is coordinated.
A multi-link mode where a device listens on several links and moves its one full radio to whichever link has traffic.
A multi-link mode where a device with several radios reassigns them between links as traffic needs.
How much radio spectrum one Wi-Fi channel occupies. Wider channels carry more data at once, but fewer of them fit in a band.
A device built for an older Wi-Fi generation. It can slow a shared channel because everyone must fall back to methods it understands.
The country or region whose radio rules apply. Each one decides which frequencies Wi-Fi may use and at what power.
A class of 6 GHz access points limited to indoor use at low power, allowed across the whole US 6 GHz band without a coordination service.
The way Wi-Fi encodes bits into a radio signal. Higher orders, such as 4096-QAM, pack more bits into each signal but need a cleaner, stronger signal.
One of the many narrow frequencies that make up a Wi-Fi channel. Each carries a few bits at a time, in parallel with the others.
Skipping a busy slice inside a wide channel so the rest of the channel can still be used, instead of falling back to a narrower channel.
A block of subcarriers within a channel that an access point assigns to one device for a transmission. Also called an RU.
A Wi-Fi 7 feature that lets one device be given several resource units in the same transmission, including ones that are not next to each other.
A Wi-Fi 6 technique that divides a channel into resource units so several devices can send or receive in the same transmission.
The previous generation of Wi-Fi security. Its password-based mode lets a recorded sign-in be attacked offline.
The current generation of Wi-Fi security, with a sign-in that resists offline password guessing and stronger encryption options.
The WPA3 sign-in exchange. Both sides prove they know the password without revealing anything an eavesdropper could test offline.
A property where learning a password later does not let someone decrypt traffic they recorded earlier, because each session used its own key.
Encryption for open networks, such as guest Wi-Fi, that protects each device's traffic without needing a password.
A security feature that lets devices check that the access point announcements they hear are genuine, not forged.
